transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-07-19
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramirez (Redwood SE), Sonia Patel (Aurelia Eng Mgr), Ken Wu (Aurelia ML), Harper Li (Aurelia DevOps), Alex Morgan (Aurelia Product)

Summary (auto): Quickstart + environment walkthrough for Redwood API/Console and developer toolchain. Focus: auth & secrets, sandbox provisioning, quick SDK examples (Python / TypeScript), and next steps for a short performance POC. Questions on VPC/private deploy, KMS, and batching.

Topics: onboarding, auth (API keys / SSO), sandbox provisioning, console quickstart, SDK snippets (py/ts), Optimize suggestions, private deployment constraints, benchmarking plan.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, really appreciate you making time, quick round of intros real fast?
[00:12] Sonia Patel: hi, this is Sonia, engineering manager for Aurelia's search product, uh we own the feature that needs LLMs.
[00:17] Ken Wu: Ken here, staff ML, I'll be doing the POC work.
[00:20] Harper Li: Harper, infra/devops, happy to talk networking and security.
[00:24] Diego Ramirez: Diego from Redwood, I'm gonna run through the console and the SDK bits.
[00:28] Maya Chen: and I am Maya, AE, I'll handle next steps and procurement questions.

[00:42] Maya Chen: quick agenda: 1) walk through console quickstart, 2) SDK examples in python and typescript, 3) auth and sandbox provisioning, 4) Optimize recommendations and benchmarking plan, 5) Q&A and next steps. sound ok?
[00:55] Sonia Patel: yes that's perfect.

[01:10] Diego Ramirez: okay opening the console — so here's the org page, we usually create a sandbox org for POCs, gives you isolated usage and temporary keys, um the link i'll share after is redwood.ai/console-quickstart (note: example link). you can see the model catalog here, open models, redwood-verified profiles, you can pin model versions for stable rollouts.
[01:40] Ken Wu: when you say pin model versions, is that per-route or per-environment?
[01:45] Diego Ramirez: good question — both. you can pin at route level in the API config or at service level in the dedicated pool for consistent performance. that's important for canary rollouts.

[02:10] Harper Li: on sandbox — what's the network footprint, do we need VPC peering, static IPs, or open egress?
[02:18] Diego Ramirez: for hosted sandbox usually no VPC peering — it's on our managed infra and you access via TLS endpoints and API keys. if you need private deployment or VPC, that's part of Redwood Private, we do VPC peering and support IP allowlists and private control plane. we'll send the Private checklist.

[02:42] Maya Chen: buyer/timing question for Sonia: what's your ideal timeline for a POC and what success metrics?
[02:50] Sonia Patel: aim for two weeks for initial integration, want to measure latency p95 under expected QPS and unit cost per session and quality — F1/accuracy for the rerank and hallucination rate on our prompts.

[03:10] Diego Ramirez: perfect, for latency p95 we usually recommend starting with a small batch of sample prompts and 3 model variants: a faster quantized small model, a balanced medium, and a higher quality unfine tuned larger model — that helps map latency/cost/quality tradeoffs.

[03:36] Ken Wu: how are keys rotated and can we use KMS/HSM?
[03:40] Diego Ramirez: hosted API keys are rotatable via the console and we integrate with customer KMS for Private deployment. for hosted we can do bring-your-own-KMS in VPC-mode for enterprise customers, otherwise we manage keys but provide envelope encryption and audit logs.

[04:02] Harper Li: audit logs — retention and access? we need 1 year for our compliance.
[04:07] Maya Chen: we have add-on observability retention, and we can extend log retention for enterprise plans — we'll include the SOC2 and logs SLA details in the doc pack.

[04:30] Diego Ramirez: switching to SDKs — small python example: from redwood import RedwoodClient, client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.environ['REDWOOD_KEY']), response = client.text.generate(model='rw-medium-1', prompt="Summarize..." ) — and similar in typescript we show the fetch example with Authorization header. we'll share code snippets.
[04:57] Ken Wu: do you have official libs or community maintained?
[05:00] Diego Ramirez: official maintained libs for python and typescript, we also publish examples for common frameworks. the libs handle streaming, function calling, and structured outputs.

[05:18] Sonia Patel: on local CI / secrets, is there guidance for rotating keys in CI and limiting environment access?
[05:24] Diego Ramirez: yep, we recommend CI with scoped service keys that only allow read/generate and restrict to specific models/routes, also using secrets manager with short TTL tokens. we'll include a CI best-practice doc in the follow-up.

[05:46] Harper Li: for private deployment, does Redwood ship an on-prem package or is it only VPC?
[05:50] Diego Ramirez: both: VPC-based private control plane and an optional on-prem bundle for air-gapped environments. on-prem supports KMS/HSM integration and local audit logs. note some kernel-level optimizations require specific GPU drivers — we'll share the hardware checklist.

[06:12] Maya Chen: ok moving to Optimize — Diego can you explain a couple of quick knobs that typically reduce cost?
[06:18] Diego Ramirez: Sure. primary levers: batching and prefix / KV caching — caching common prefixes or context reduces tokens. second: quantization profiles — moving from fp16 to int8/4 when quality tolerates it. third: model routing — route low criticality calls to cheaper variants. our Optimize tool will suggest batching sizes and quant profiles based on sampled traffic.

[06:46] Ken Wu: any quick rule of thumb for latency tradeoffs with batching?
[06:50] Diego Ramirez: continuous batching is workload-aware; for sub-100ms SLOs keep batch windows small, but for high throughput you can tolerate a 20-50ms batch buffer to reduce cost significantly. we'll include a small spreadsheet with simulated SLO vs unit cost.

[07:12] Sonia Patel: can we run a quick local test — like you provision sandbox keys and we try a small sample?
[07:18] Maya Chen: yes that's the plan — we'll provision a sandbox and Diego will run a pairing session to run basic throughput/latency checks.

[07:30] Diego Ramirez: now i'm going to paste the code snippet for typescript: const resp = await fetch('https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate',{method:'POST', headers:{'Authorization':`Bearer ${process.env.REDWOOD_KEY}`}, body: JSON.stringify({model:'rw-medium-1', input:'...'} )}) response.json()
[07:52] Ken Wu: do you support streaming over websockets or SSE?
[07:55] Diego Ramirez: streaming via SSE and websocket clients, and our TS lib exposes an async iterator. there's also native streaming support in the console for debugging.

[08:12] Alex Morgan: product question — can we attach metadata to requests and have it appear in Console traces?
[08:17] Diego Ramirez: yes you can attach arbitrary route-level metadata and tags which show up in Console traces and cost breakdowns.

[08:30] Sonia Patel: about rate limits — if we burst during peak periods, do you have graceful fallback? we prefer a model failover to cheaper model rather than 429.
[08:37] Maya Chen: Redwood supports routing policies with automated fallback to compatible model variants and burst capacity settings for Dedicated customers. for hosted we can set soft-quotas and alerts.

[08:55] Harper Li: what's the expected onboarding work for us? firewall, allowlist, CI updates?
[09:00] Diego Ramirez: minimal for hosted: allow outbound TLS to our endpoints, add keys to secrets manager, update CI to use scoped keys. for private: VPC, peering, or a transit gateway and some routing rules plus KMS setup. we'll provide a step-by-step checklist.

[09:20] Sonia Patel: do you have any pre-built reranker examples? we run candidate generation + rerank pipeline.
[09:24] Diego Ramirez: yes, we have rerank model examples and a small retrain/finetune workflow in labs. we also recommend using structured outputs to reduce hallucinations and a rerank scoring function with prompt templates — will share sample prompts.

[09:46] Ken Wu: logging costs — token-level cost breakdown at trace level, right?
[09:50] Diego Ramirez: yes Console gives token-level cost, per-route and per-model breakdowns. you can also export traces to an S3 or SIEM.

[10:05] Alex Morgan: any blockers for us to start the POC? what do you need from Aurelia?
[10:10] Maya Chen: we'll need prompt set, QPS targets, and a list of stakeholders for the pairing session. Harper will provide network constraints.

[10:22] Harper Li: i'll get you a short list of IP allowlist constraints and our proxy behavior.

[10:28] Diego Ramirez: quick note — we sometimes see misspellings in the models when auto-transcription hits the slide — like K-V cache gets written as K-V cash, so don't worry if the transcript looks odd.

[10:40] Sonia Patel: ha yes.

[10:50] Maya Chen: ok let's verbalize next steps: 1) Maya sends SOC2 + KMS doc and console quickstart 2) Diego prepares benchmark plan and quick quant profiles 3) Redwood provisions sandbox org and API keys 4) Aurelia provides prompt set and network constraints 5) schedule POC pairing session next week.

[11:15] Ken Wu: timeline sounds good to me.
[11:20] Maya Chen: any final compliance questions?
[11:24] Harper Li: just to confirm audit log retention options and access controls, we'll review the whitepaper.

[11:35] Maya Chen: great, we'll follow up in email with attachments. thanks everyone.
[11:40] Diego Ramirez: thanks all, i'll send code snippets and the small spreadsheet.

[11:48] Meeting end: 15:52 UTC

Notes: transcript contains natural disfluencies and occasional minor mis-attributions; some proper nouns spelled phonetically as occurs in auto transcripts. Links and artifacts referenced: Console quickstart (link), SOC2 whitepaper, KMS integration notes, benchmarking spreadsheet, python and typescript code snippets.
